name: Glasses to mask facial flaws
lead: Glasses to mask facial flaws is a style practice of wearing frames chosen to draw attention away from features a person dislikes, such as under-eye bags, asymmetry or the nose, and toward the eyes and frame. Thick, large or darker frames are the ones most often described for this purpose, and the aim is a face that reads as more balanced and put-together.[1]

Glasses are often chosen for how they change the wearer's appearance, and some people with good eyesight wear them purely as a style accessory. Frames come in many shapes, colors and materials, from aviator, browline and horn-rimmed to rimless, and consumers increasingly buy non-prescription lenses as fashion accessories.[1]

Research on glasses has mostly examined how they change social impressions rather than whether they conceal specific features. A 2011 set of experiments in the Swiss Journal of Psychology found that adding glasses to faces raised ratings of intelligence and success, while effects on attractiveness and trustworthiness depended on frame type.[2] No studies were found testing whether frames conceal or change the perception of particular features such as eye bags or nose shape.

angle.text: People choose frames to frame the eyes, add structure to the upper face and divert attention from features they dislike. Frame choice also changes how the face is perceived socially, for example as more intelligent or successful.

infobox: Aviator, browline, horn-rimmed, rimless, Wayfarer and others[1]

paras: Frames come in many styles and materials, and many consumers buy non-prescription glasses as accessories.[1] Appearance communities discuss thick frames as a way to cover under-eye bags or distract from asymmetry. Lens shape involves trade-offs: higher-power lenses are thicker in large shapes.[1]

For most of their history glasses were seen as unfashionable, and wearers were stereotyped as clergy, elderly or physically weak. In the 1930s spectacles were still described as medical appliances; the stigma began to fade in the early 1900s in the US, helped by figures such as Theodore Roosevelt and Harold Lloyd. Buddy Holly and John Lennon popularized particular frame styles, and fashionable frames became widely available from manufacturers in the 1970s.[1] Eyewear is now treated like other fashion goods, with designers, labels and seasonal collections.[1]

sections.h: Perception of people who wear glasses
paras: Wikipedia describes a halo effect linking glasses with intelligence, and reports studies finding that wearing glasses boosted politicians' electoral success in Western cultures. Some people wear non-prescription glasses purely for their image.[1]

In Experiment 1 of a 2011 paper by Leder, Forster and Gerger, 76 participants rated 78 face images shown without glasses, with full-rim glasses and with rimless glasses. Both glasses types raised ratings of intelligence and success. Full-rim glasses were rated less attractive than no glasses, while rimless glasses showed no attractiveness difference and were rated more trustworthy.[2]
No studies found testing whether frames conceal or change the perception of eye bags, asymmetry or nose shape. Research on perception of faces with glasses is described above.[2]

timeline.event: Spectacles still described as medical appliances.[1]

card.summary: Using chunky frames to hide bags, asymmetry or a nose; a styling trick with no research behind it.
card.note: Perceived effect is subjective and untested.

quick.overview:
Some people wear thick or oversized frames to take attention away from features they dislike, such as under-eye bags, asymmetry or the nose.

No studies were found testing whether this changes how a face is perceived.
quick.mechanism: Frames add visual weight around the eyes and nose bridge, which proponents say redirects the viewer's attention.
quick.risks: No health risks. Results depend on the person and are not measured.
